newsitem.title: UK: S&P cuts Burns Philip outlook to negative.
newsitem.headline: S&P cuts Burns Philip outlook to negative.

text.p: Standard & Poor's said on Wednesday it had revised its rating outlook on Burns, Philp & Co. Ltd (BPC) to negative from stable, and affirmed the BBB plus/A2 ratings of the company.
"The outlook revision reflects BPC's weakened operating performance in its highly competitive global markets," S&P said.
"The ratings could be downgraded if the company is unable to improve operating performance and financial measure steadily over the next two years," S&P said.

"The company's overall financial profile is weak for the current ratings. A new management structure has been established to address the competition, but meaningful improvement is not expected in the short term. The ratings continue to reflect the company's position as a major supplier in the global markets of yeast and food ingredients.

As an Australian-based, global food ingredients company, BPC has a network of manufacturing and marketing operations across over 32 countries, although key markets remain in the U.S., Europe, and Australia. Its yeast and food ingredients products service both industrial and consumer markets, providing both geographic and modest product diversity.

BPC has about 16% of the world's bakers yeast market, which is marginally ahead of the second- largest producer. Although the market is highly price-competitive and sensitive to raw materials cost, the majority of BPC's yeast volume is sold to low-margin, but relatively stable, industrial bakery customers.

Heightened competition in Australia following entry of new competitor has been mitigated by higher growth in South America and Asia. BPC has moved aggressively into the global spice market since 1994 by large acquisitions, particularly in North America.

Although the branded spice products should attract higher operating margin, the majority of BPC's spice business is exposed to the highly competitive U.S. consumer market, which is led by the U.S.-based McCormick & Co. Inc. Price competition between the two companies for supermarket shelf and market share has resulted in BPC's weak operating performance in fiscal 1996.

This also is reflected in A$140 million abnormal charges in fiscal 1996, which includes write-down of unprofitable slotting contracts at A$34 million in North America, launch costs of unsuccessful consumer products in North America at A$10 million, start-up costs mostly related to market development in Asia at A$19 million, and business rationalization costs at A$55 million.

Nevertheless, consolidation of North American spice operations onto the Ankeny plant, and centralization of the European consumer spice operations in Ostmann, should improve cost efficiency for BPC in fiscal 1997. Although BPC has a relatively stable leverage, both interest cover (pretax interest cover at about 2 times) and cash flow protection (funds from operations-to-total debt about 15%) are weak for the ratings.

The outlook reflects the company's difficulty in improving operating performance in the short term, particularly in the U.S. consumer spice market, slower-than-anticipated benefits from acquisitions, and weak cash flow protection. The new management structure is yet to demonstrate ability to improve profitability in the global businesses.
